description: Welcome to the AutoNav Lite Project!
summary: AutoNav is an extended offline-first, open-source take on NASA Mars Trek that can be deployed on low-power devices for Martian missions. The app's exclusive feature is to plan paths from point A to point B depending on various requirements such as shortest path, minimal wheel damage and dead-zone prevention. While there are many advanced sensor-fusion approaches for optimizing trajectories, this project would be one of the open-source ideas developed on NASA's datasets.

GITHUB URL : https://github.com/iamshan794/AutoNavLite


MOTIVATION

1. Sand traps look like safe, flat ground: Opportunity spent five weeks digging out of the "Purgatory" ripple (2005), and Spirit ended its driving career in soft soil at "Troy" (2009). Imagery and slope maps cannot tell loose fines from firm ground at the same slope.

2. Sharp rocks wear out wheels: Curiosity's 0.75 mm aluminium wheel skins were punctured by wind-carved rocks on otherwise flat plains. The cheapest route is not always the kindest to the wheels.

3. Communication dead zones: Relay orbiters are only useful well above the horizon. Crater walls, canyon floors and large mounds hide part of the sky, and an astronaut on an EVA cannot afford to drop out of contact.

4. Position drift forces stop-and-wait: Wheel slip makes odometry drift; once position uncertainty grows too large, the rover must stop and re-localise against orbital maps.

5. Terrain classification helps navigation: Knowing whether the ground ahead is dunes, cliffs, gullies or smooth plains turns a raw elevation map into a map a planner (and a crew) can reason about.

SUMMARY

AutoNav Lite is fundamentally a UNIX service designed to run on low-power devices with minimal memory and bandwidth use for long-range missions. It runs in three modes, depending on the device's budget:

- Headless mode: the autonav0d service on its own. Any client (curl, scripts, other tools) sends source and destination lat/lon to the HTTP API (or a Unix socket) and gets route profiles back as GeoJSON.

- 2D mode: a lightweight web map similar to trek.nasa.gov. Pick a start and a goal on the map and compare the generated routes side by side, with their elevation profiles.

- 3D mode: an extension of 2D mode. It drapes the map on 3D Martian terrain, draws the routes on it and gives a 3D fly-along preview of the rover's or astronaut's path.

All modes run offline, so the system keeps working when the device itself sits in a comm dead zone.

PATH PLANNING

Routes are planned with A* on a grid built from NASA's MOLA elevation data. Each route profile uses a different cost:

- Shortest: distance (45° physical slope limit).

- Safe rover: gentle slopes, avoiding soft ground and comm dead zones.

- Wheel saver: least wheel wear (slope load, roughness, rocky ground, sharp turns).

- Astronaut EVA: walking time (Tobler's hiking function), staying in comm coverage.

Every route reports distance, ascent, maximum slope, EVA hours, rover sols and energy, a wheel-wear index, km through poor or no comms, and where the rover should stop to re-localise. Routes can be compared Google-Maps-style, including against the paths historic rovers actually drove.

Comm dead zones: computed from terrain. For every elevation cell, the horizon is traced in 16 directions; if crater walls or mountains block too much of the sky above 10°, relay passes are lost and the cell is marked reduced, poor or dead.

Terrain classes: produced by a classifier trained on DoMars16k (Wilhelm et al., 2020, CC BY 4.0), about 16,000 labelled 200×200 px orbital CTX images in 15 landform classes, grouped into five families:

- Aeolian bedforms: straight and curved dunes and ripples (soft-ground risk).

- Topographic landforms: cliffs, ridges, channels, mounds.

- Slope features: gullies, slope streaks, mass wasting.

- Impact landforms: craters, crater fields.

- Basic terrain: smooth, rough, textured, mixed.

Model: a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 backbone (Meta, Apache-2.0) extracts image features, and a small linear head trained locally maps them to the 15 classes. Training takes minutes on a single consumer GPU (RTX 5060), and the head is under 100 KB. On the held-out DoMars16k test set it reaches 89.5% accuracy (86.7–89% on imagery degraded to the map's resolution). The model is run once, offline, over NASA Trek CTX mosaics of the rover sites and candidate human landing zones; the resulting class maps (250–500 m cells, a few hundred KB each) ship with the app. Each class tells the planner how risky it is: dunes count as soft ground, cliffs and rough terrain as rocky, smooth plains as safe.

FUTURE WORK

- Add points of interest to the map:

- Geotag Perseverance images to the rover's location.

- Plot seismic activity and triangulate epicentres.

- Overlay weather and surface-composition data.

- Extend the 3D view with visual SLAM.

- Integrate hillshade (sun illumination and shadows) into the 3D view and path planning to prevent shadow zones.
